questions.q: Decompose split the weather spec into 9 components across 2 waves. Wave 0 holds WeatherDataModel, WeatherService, HealthzHandler, APIConfig, ErrorHandlingMiddleware, RateLimitMiddleware and WeatherTestSuite; Wave 1 holds WeatherHandler and RootPageHandler. What determines which wave a given component lands in?
options: Its estimated complexity band: low-complexity components are scheduled into the earliest waves so that every wave finishes close to its 10-minute floor.
Its component type: models, services, configs, middleware and tests always go in Wave 0, and handlers always go in the last wave, whatever the dependency edges say.
The depth of its dependency chain: a component lands in the first wave by which every component it depends on has already been built.
The alphabetical order of its component id, which keeps decompose deterministic across repeated runs of the same dense spec.
questions.explanation: Waves come out of a topological sort (Kahn's algorithm) over the dependency graph: each wave is the set of components whose dependencies were all satisfied by an earlier wave. The Decompose page's dependency graph shows the edges for this plan. weather-handler depends on weather-service, error-middleware and rate-limit-middleware, and root-page-handler depends on error-middleware, so both handlers have to wait for Wave 0. Type does not decide placement: HealthzHandler is also a handler, but it depends on nothing, so it sits in Wave 0. Complexity cannot be what separates the waves either, because all 9 components are rated medium; complexity only feeds the time estimate. Even the wave title is not evidence. 'Foundation (Models + Config)' is the fixed name the decomposer always gives the second wave, which is why it sits above two handlers here. Ordering within a wave means nothing, since everything in a wave runs at the same time.

questions.q: The build package metadata reads `total_components: 9`, `total_waves: 2`, `max_parallelism: 7`. Wave 0 has 7 components and Wave 1 has 2. Where does the 7 come from, and what consumes it?
options: The average wave size (9 ÷ 2, rounded up), which the Build Agent uses to decide how many waves it may keep in flight at once.
The size of the largest wave; the Build Agent reads it from the package metadata and uses it as the thread-pool worker cap for every wave.
The number of distinct component types in the plan; it is a reporting metric only, and the Build Agent ignores it at run time.
A fixed default that the Decompose page writes into every build package, which the Build Agent ignores in favour of one worker per CPU core.
questions.explanation: Max parallelism is the width of the widest wave, here Wave 0 with its 7 components. It is not an average: 9 ÷ 2 rounded up is 5. It is not the count of component types either, because this plan has 6 (model, service, handler, config, middleware, test). And it is not a fixed default: earlier decompose runs of the same weather spec reported 3 and 6. The Build Agent reads `max_parallelism` from the package metadata and passes it to its thread pool as the worker count. That is why all 7 Wave 0 prompts went to the model at once, while Wave 1 used 2 of the 7 workers. Waves never run at the same time as each other, because Wave 1's components need Wave 0's output, so a knob for 'how many waves at once' would have nothing to control.

questions.q: Decompose estimated 180 min one-by-one versus 40 min in waves (78% saved) for 9 medium-complexity components in 2 waves. The real build then finished in 105.8s. Per-component times were, for Wave 0: weather-data-model 64.3s, error-middleware 63.1s, test-suite 60.6s, healthz-handler 42.9s, weather-service 23.5s, rate-limit-middleware 14.0s, api-config 2.6s; and for Wave 1: weather-handler 41.6s, root-page-handler 18.2s. Which statement explains both the estimate and the measured total?
options: Both numbers are averages: 40 min is the 180 min divided across the 7 workers, and 105.8s is the mean component time multiplied by the number of waves.
The estimate comes from timing the model on the previous run of the same spec, and 105.8s is that estimate after the Build Agent subtracts network overhead.
The Build Agent sends all 9 prompts at once to its 7 workers, so the total is the time for the first 7 calls plus the 2 calls that queued behind them.

A wave takes as long as its slowest component: the estimate is 20 + 20 = 40 min against 9 × 20 = 180 min, and the build took 64.3s + 41.6s ≈ 105.8s, about a third of the 330.8s that all nine calls add up to.
questions.explanation: Decompose gives every component a fixed estimate from its complexity band (low 10 min, medium 20, high 30). The one-by-one figure adds up all of them (9 × 20 = 180). The wave figure adds up only the slowest member of each wave (20 + 20 = 40), because a wave lasts as long as its longest component. That is a static estimate made before any model call, and it says nothing about a particular machine. The measured build has the same shape: Wave 0's slowest component took 64.3s and Wave 1's took 41.6s, and 64.3 + 41.6 ≈ 105.8s. The averages do not work: 180 ÷ 7 is about 26, not 40, and the mean component time (36.8s) times 2 waves is ≈ 73.5s, not 105.8. If Wave 1 had only queued for a free worker, it would have started when api-config finished at 2.6s, and the build would have ended near 64.3s. Because every component is medium, the shortcut (9 − 2) ÷ 9 also happens to give 78%; that shortcut only matches when all components share one complexity band.

questions.q: In the build package, WeatherHandler (Wave 1) has `consumes: WeatherService`, and its prompt ends with `Depends on (import, do not implement): WeatherService`. This is a Python build. What happens to that dependency when the Build Agent generates weather-handler.py?
options: The line is passed through unchanged, and the model writes an import of WeatherService from weather-service.py, which the app shell makes importable by putting src/ on the Python path.

Decompose has already used the dependency to place WeatherHandler in Wave 1. For Python the Build Agent strips the 'Depends on' line and tells the file it cannot import other generated files, so the handler implements the weather call itself, with the spec's API and error rules pasted into its prompt.
The Build Agent waits for weather-service.py, then inlines its source into the weather-handler prompt so the model can copy the service code into the handler file word for word.
The component fails validation, because in Python builds a Wave 1 component is not allowed to depend on a Wave 0 component, and the build carries on without it.
questions.explanation: Python component files are named with hyphens (weather-service.py), and the app shell loads each one on its own, so one generated file can never import another. The Build Agent therefore removes the 'Depends on (import, do not implement)' line from Python prompts and adds a rule in its place: do not import project modules, do not write mocks or stubs for them, and implement everything the file needs with the allowed packages. Handlers also receive an 'Application spec' excerpt (Purpose, API, Error Handling, Data Model, Security, Performance), because each handler must implement its routes completely on its own. The edge still matters for ordering, since it is why WeatherHandler sits in Wave 1, but it no longer means code reuse. The cost: WeatherService, WeatherDataModel and APIConfig are still generated, but nothing makes the handler use them. In run 2 of this same spec, the service, client and model files ended up unused. No source is inlined from another component, and nothing fails: a Wave 1 component depending on Wave 0 is exactly what waves are for.

questions.q: Each entry under `dag:` in the build package is what the Build Agent works from for one component, and this plan has 9 entries. What does a single entry contain?
options: The entire dense spec, so the model generating that component has the full architectural picture and can resolve any constraint that its own description leaves implicit.
Just the component name and its target language; the Build Agent looks up the role, constraints and dependencies from the Decompose page at generation time.
Its name, type, wave and complexity band, only the spec constraints that apply to it, any component it consumes, and a prompt built from its purpose and those constraints.
Its prompt plus the expected file contents, so the model can diff its own output against the reference target and correct itself before it returns.
questions.explanation: Each entry is a deliberately narrow slice. HealthzHandler's entry carries a single constraint, 'GET /healthz returns 200.' ErrorHandlingMiddleware's carries the four status-code rules (400, 404, 502, 500), and WeatherHandler's lists `consumes: WeatherService`. The full dense spec appears once, under `spec:` at the top of the file, for people and the orchestrator to read. It is not copied into each entry, because giving every component the whole spec brings back the problem decomposition exists to prevent. The Build Agent adds more detail later, outside the package: the target path, runtime and allowed packages for every file, and, for Python handlers, an excerpt of the spec's API and error rules, because a handler must implement its route on its own. There is no reference implementation to diff against, because the file does not exist yet.

questions.q: The Build Agent's Wrap Prompt stage wraps the decompose-supplied component prompt before it reaches the LLM. What does the wrapper add?
options: The target file path, the runtime version, the list of packages already installed in the image, and a file-shape template for that component type and language.
The full dense spec, the wave plan, the dependency graph and every interface contract, so each component is generated with exactly the context the orchestrator holds.
A system prompt, a sampling temperature, a token budget and a stop sequence, all tuned per component type and language so a two-line config file is not sampled like a service.
The Dockerfile, the package.json and the .env.example already written for this run, so the model can see the project layout it is emitting a file into.
questions.explanation: The wrapper exists to make the output mechanically usable, not to hand over the whole architecture. For run 5's weather-handler it names the exact target file (`src/weather-handler.py`) and pins the runtime (Python 3.12). It lists the packages actually installed in the image (`flask`, `requests`; test files also get `pytest`), so the model cannot import something that will not resolve, and it pastes a shape template for that component type and language. It opens with `Output the file CONTENTS ONLY — no markdown fences, no prose`, an instruction inside the prompt text, not a sampling parameter. Python builds get more on top. Every non-test file gets a list of rules: do not import other generated files, no stubs or placeholders, read environment variables at request time, never log, return or render a secret. Handlers also get an excerpt of the spec's Purpose, API, Error Handling, Data Model, Security and Performance lines, because each handler must implement its routes on its own. What the wrapper never adds is the wave plan, the dependency graph or other components' code, and it adds no interface contracts either. The Dockerfile and requirements.txt do not exist yet at this stage; Assemble writes them after the components are generated.

questions.q: Run 5's build has two waves: Wave 0 (weather-data-model, weather-service, healthz-handler, api-config, error-middleware, rate-limit-middleware, test-suite) and Wave 1 (weather-handler, root-page-handler). Every component succeeded on its first attempt. How many LLM calls did the Build Agent make, and in what pattern?
options: One call for the whole build: the model emits all nine files in a single response, which is what keeps their imports consistent.
Two calls, one per wave, each returning that wave's files together so the components in a wave can reference each other.
Nine calls, all submitted at once to the 7-worker pool; the two Wave 1 calls simply queue until a worker frees up.
Nine calls, one per component: Wave 0's seven are sent at the same time, and only once all seven have returned are Wave 1's two sent at the same time.
questions.explanation: One LLM call per component is the unit of isolation: each call sees only its own component's prompt, so a bad generation stays contained to one file. Within a wave, the calls go to a thread pool sized by max_parallelism (7) and run at the same time. Between waves, the agent blocks until every call in the wave has returned, because Wave 1's components were placed there precisely because they depend on Wave 0. The timings show it. If Wave 1 had only queued for a free worker, it would have started when api-config finished after 2.6s, and the build would have ended near 64.3s. Instead it took 105.8s, which is Wave 0's slowest (weather-data-model, 64.3s) plus Wave 1's slowest (weather-handler, 41.6s). If a component's output had failed the validity checks, the Build Agent would have made one more call for that component with the rejection reason appended. No retries were needed in this run.

questions.q: The Python Dockerfile the Build Agent writes ends with `CMD ["python", "src/app.py"]`, but a decompose-derived build package usually contains no `app` component. What does the Assemble stage do about that?
options: It rewrites the Dockerfile's CMD to point at whichever generated file looks most like an entrypoint, preferring one that calls `app.run()` and falling back to the first `src/*.py` that registers a Blueprint route at module level.

It writes an `src/app.py` shim — only if the build did not already generate one — that creates the Flask app, auto-registers every module-level Blueprint found in sibling `src/*.py` files, and always serves `/healthz`.

It fails the build with an explicit error telling the user to add an `app` component to the build package, on the grounds that silently inventing an entrypoint would hide a real gap in the decompose output from whoever has to run the build.

It concatenates every generated Python file into a single `src/app.py`, in dependency order and with duplicate imports hoisted to the top, so the fixed CMD resolves without the Assemble stage having to write a line of code of its own.
questions.explanation: The generated components are Flask *fragments* — a `Blueprint(...)` plus `@bp.get(...)` handlers — with no `Flask(__name__)` and no `app.run()`. With a fixed CMD and no `src/app.py`, the container dies on start with `can't open file '/app/src/app.py'`. The shim supplies the missing assembly layer without editing a single generated file, and the existence check means a build that genuinely produced its own entrypoint keeps it rather than being overwritten. The always-on `/healthz` is not decoration: it guarantees the Kubernetes probe has something to hit even when no generated handler exposed a health route. Concatenating files would still duplicate route registrations and collide on module-level names however carefully the imports were tidied up; rewriting the CMD per build would make the image's start command unpredictable.

questions.q: For one component, the LLM returns the text "I cannot generate this file without more information about your database schema." What does the Build Agent do?
options: Writes the returned text to the target source file anyway; the Docker build will catch it later.
Retries the same prompt at a higher sampling temperature until code comes back, capped at three attempts.

Rejects it and writes no file, sends the same prompt once more with the rejection reason appended, and if that answer is also rejected marks the component failed while the rest of the build carries on.
Substitutes a stub satisfying the component's declared interface so the wave still ends green.
questions.explanation: Post-processing is a validity gate, not a formatter. If the response is fenced, the first fenced block is extracted. If it is unfenced, the first non-blank line must begin with a code-like token (`import`, `from`, `def`, `class`, `const`, `export`, and so on). Prose fails both tests, so the output is rejected and nothing is written. For Python, accepted code must also parse, and it must not contain stub markers such as `TODO` or `placeholder`. A rejection triggers exactly one more call, with the same prompt, the same sampling settings and the reason appended ('Your previous output was rejected: ...'). That is the only automatic retry; there is no temperature change. If the second answer is also rejected, the component is reported as an error with attempts 2, and no file is written for it. The other components in the wave still finish, and later waves still run. The Build page is coded to show a red failure banner and hide the 'Continue to Deploy' link in that case, so recovering a failed component is a human decision: rebuild. Deferring the failure to the Docker build would turn a clear per-component error into a confusing one later, and substituting a stub is exactly the happy-path faking the stub check exists to block. In run 5 all 9 components passed on the first attempt.

questions.q: A JavaScript build of 4 components finishes. Which files exist in that run's workspace folder?
options: Only the 4 generated `src/*.js` files — packaging is the Deploy Agent's job, and it reads the workspace directly when it renders the deploy YAML.
The 4 generated `src/*.js` files plus a `Dockerfile`, a `package.json`, a `.env.example`, and an `src/app-server.js` entrypoint if none was generated.
The 4 generated files plus a Helm chart and a rendered Kubernetes Deployment manifest, written at assemble time so the Deploy Agent only has to apply them.
The 4 generated files plus a per-component test suite and a GitHub Actions CI workflow, both emitted by Assemble so the build is verified before the image is pushed.
questions.explanation: Assemble writes the project-level files the generated sources cannot produce for themselves: a language-appropriate Dockerfile (`node:20-alpine`, `EXPOSE 3000`, `CMD ["node","src/app-server.js"]`), a dependency manifest listing exactly the packages the prompt told the model it was allowed to use (`package.json` for JavaScript, `requirements.txt` for Python), a `.env.example` naming the secrets a developer still has to supply, and the entrypoint shim when the build did not generate one. Kubernetes YAML is rendered later by the Deploy Agent from a template, against the workspace — it is not a build artefact. Tests and CI workflows are never emitted anywhere in this pipeline; that is Module 5's subject.

questions.q: The Deploy Agent fills in `healthcheck_path` in the rendered YAML; in run 5 it chose `/healthz`. How does it choose the path, and what happens if it finds no GET route at all?
options: It starts the container locally on a scratch port, probes each candidate path in turn, and records whichever one returns 200, so the manifest always names a path the image has already answered on.
It reads the path out of the dense spec's Deployment section, which is where intake records hosting details, and falls back to `/health` whenever that field was left blank.
It refuses to render: an empty health path is a hard error, so you must add a health route and rebuild before the Deploy page will show any YAML at all.

It scans the generated sources for GET route literals and takes the first hit from a fixed priority list (`/healthz`, `/health`, `/readyz`, `/ready`, `/ping`, `/`), else the shortest route found; with no route at all, the Deploy page falls back to `/`.
questions.explanation: The derivation is a static scan of the workspace for `.get('...')` route registrations, resolved against a fixed preference order. If none of the preferred paths exist, it uses the shortest route it found. In a Python build the scan normally succeeds, because the Build Agent's `src/app.py` shim registers `@app.get("/healthz")` itself. That is why run 5's YAML says `/healthz`, and why handler prompts are told not to define it. The renderer does reject an empty path, but the Deploy page passes `/` whenever the scan returns nothing, so rendering never blocks. A `/` probe is only safe if the app answers 200 there, because a 404 fails a readiness probe. Kubernetes would then mark the pod unready, and the mistake would surface minutes later as a rollout that never completes. Nothing can be probed at render time, because no container is running yet. The spec's Deployment section describes hosting (in run 5: 'fubo platform', the `training` namespace), not routes.

questions.q: Two different apps are built and deployed through the pipeline. What do they share in ECR, and what keeps them from colliding?
options: Both push to the same `architect-builds/app` repository; only the image tag is per-run unique, and nothing collides because the Kubernetes Application name and ingress host are still derived from the spec slug plus run id.

Nothing is shared — each app gets its own ECR repository named after its spec slug, so the repo-creation pre-flight runs once per app and two apps can never write into the same registry path at all, not even during a concurrent build.

They share both the repository and the tag, so the newer push simply overwrites the older image; that is safe here because the Kubernetes Application object is deleted and recreated on every deploy and never references an overwritten image.

They share both the repository and the tag, and the Kubernetes Application name is randomly generated on each run, which is the mechanism that keeps the two running deployments and their ingress hosts from overwriting one another on the cluster.
questions.explanation: The registry path is deliberately kept separate from the app. With one shared repository, the ECR repo-creation pre-flight happens once ever instead of once per new app, and does nothing on every later build. Uniqueness lives in two other places. The image tag carries the short run id (`architect-builds/app:bd56da`), so images never overwrite each other. The Kubernetes Application name and the ingress host carry the app identity (`app-bd56da`, `app-bd56da-training.tools.fubotv.net`), and the app's Secret follows the same name (`app-bd56da-openweather`). In this run the build package carried no name, so the spec slug fell back to `app`, and the run id alone kept the name unique. That is exactly why the run id is always part of it. Random names would give you uniqueness without identity: you could no longer tell which running Application belongs to which app.

questions.q: The Deploy Agent always builds with `docker build --platform linux/amd64`. If that flag were dropped and the build ran on an Apple Silicon laptop, what would fail, and when?
options: `docker build` would fail immediately with an unsupported-architecture error, before any layer reached the ECR registry.
`docker push` would be rejected by ECR, which validates the image manifest's architecture against the repository's declared platform setting.
Build and push would both succeed; the pod would then sit in ImagePullBackOff on the cluster with `no match for platform in manifest`.
Nothing would fail — the kubelet emulates the mismatched architecture transparently, at a modest CPU and memory cost.
questions.explanation: This is a late-binding failure, which is exactly why the flag is pinned instead of left to the host default. Docker on an arm64 machine happily builds an arm64 image, and ECR is a content-agnostic registry with no per-repository platform to validate against, so it happily stores it — neither step has any reason to object. The mismatch is only discovered when an amd64 node's kubelet tries to pull the image and finds no matching platform in the manifest, at which point you are debugging a crash-looping pod two green steps and several minutes downstream of the actual cause. Pinning `--platform` moves the decision to the only place that knows the deployment target: the build.

questions.q: You apply a manifest in which only the image tag changed (`abc123` → `def456`); replicas stay at 2. What does the cluster actually do?
options: The API server patches the two running containers in place with the new image, which is why a tag-only change is the cheapest update there is: the kubelet pulls `def456`, swaps the image field, and the pods keep their own names, IP addresses and start times.

The Deployment controller diffs desired against actual state, creates a NEW ReplicaSet for `def456`, and the default rolling update (maxSurge 1, maxUnavailable 0) brings up a replacement and waits for its readiness probe before terminating an old pod.

Both running pods are deleted first, then two fresh pods are created from the new image, because a ReplicaSet's pod template is immutable once created and the Deployment controller has no way to overlap old and new pods inside one ReplicaSet, whatever maxSurge says.

`kubectl apply` blocks until every pod is Ready and then returns, so nothing at all happens asynchronously; if a readiness probe never passes, the apply call itself is what eventually times out and reports the rollout failure back to the caller.
questions.explanation: A pod's image cannot be edited in place, so a tag change can only be realised by creating new pods — which is why a second ReplicaSet appears and the old one is scaled to zero rather than mutated. The rolling-update defaults are what make the swap zero-downtime: maxUnavailable 0 forbids killing an old pod before its replacement reports Ready, maxSurge 1 allows exactly one extra pod during the overlap, and the Service selector routes only to Ready pods so traffic never lands on a starting container. Deleting both pods first would be a hard outage. And `apply` is asynchronous — it returns as soon as the API server has stored the desired state; observing the rollout is a separate `kubectl rollout status` call — not because a ReplicaSet's template cannot be edited, but because the Deployment controller tracks each template revision as its own ReplicaSet, which is exactly what lets old and new pods coexist during the roll.

questions.q: A pipeline run ends with a live URL returning HTTP 200. What has the pipeline verified?
options: Only that the ingress served a successful response at the derived health path — nothing about behavioural correctness, and no tests ran at any point in the pipeline.
That the generated code passes the test suite Assemble emitted for it, and that the rendered deploy config validated cleanly before it was applied.
That the app is behaviourally correct, since a 200 from the health path can only be produced by the generated handlers actually running and returning data.
That the rollout is now being monitored and will automatically roll back if the readiness probe starts failing once the poll window has closed.
questions.explanation: The only thing the pipeline itself checks is that the app answers. When the agent host can apply, it polls `https://<host>/healthz` every 5 seconds for up to 120 seconds and stops at the first 200 or 302. In the manual-apply path, the panel gives you `curl -sS https://app-bd56da-training.tools.fubotv.net/healthz` instead. No automated tests run: run 5 even generated a WeatherTestSuite component (src/test-suite.py), and nothing ran it. There is also no deploy-config validation, no health-monitoring dashboard, and no rollback or blue-green strategy; all of that is Module 5. Whether the app actually worked had to be checked by hand. The app's `GET /api/weather?city=Chicago` returned 38.3 °F against OpenWeather's own imperial 38.08 °F (a 0.22 °F difference), an unknown city returned 404, and a missing city returned 400. Run 4 shows why that check matters. Its pipeline succeeded and its page loaded with a 200, but the generated page JavaScript converted the already-Fahrenheit value a second time and showed 12 °F while the API said 53.11. A green pipeline means 'running and reachable', not 'working'.
